name: Cameralism
summary: Cameralism was the 18th-century German science of managing the territorial state: a bureaucracy trained in finance, economy and Polizei raises revenue, population and productive output for the monarch while promoting subjects' welfare. It favours state-directed economic life, import substitution and a favourable trade balance, and puts trained officials in charge under a strong monarch.
scope: The German and Austrian cameralist tradition from Seckendorff (Teutscher Fürstenstaat, 1656) through Justi, Sonnenfels and Jung-Stilling's 1788 textbook; excludes neocameralism and later welfare-state or Prussian-socialist readings. Modern topics are mostly answered by inference at low confidence.

sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Justi's modern commercial monarchies, respect for private property, tax reform, reduced guild power.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Cameralism assumed officials must steer economic life and that individuals cannot be trusted to serve the common good unaided, though later cameralists like Justi wanted fewer monopolies and guild restrictions.

public-ownership.rationale: Cameralist princes ran crown estates, mines, forests and manufactories as the core revenue base, so state ownership of productive enterprise was standard; modern utilities are an extension, hence not the strongest.

unions-good.rationale: Cameralists organized labour through state-supervised guilds and Polizei regulation, and Justi wanted to curb guild power; autonomous workers' associations would compete with the sovereign's administration.

property-fundamental.rationale: Justi held that a successful state requires moderate government respecting private property, yet cameralists also let the sovereign direct land use and economy for state ends, so property is secure but not near-absolute.

cut-welfare.rationale: Cameralists made care for the poor and the productive employment of subjects a state duty, though with work compulsion for idlers; cutting welfare for dependency reasons is not their line.

worker-ownership.rationale: Cameralism was a top-down administrative doctrine in which the sovereign and his officials organize production; collective ownership by workers has no place in its sources.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Cameralist Polizei relied on census, registers and close information gathering about every subject, and Jung-Stilling treats policing of dangerous sects as normal state practice.

strong-leader.rationale: The cameralist model is a strong monarch acting through an efficient bureaucracy to reform the country without estates blocking him; Justi judged only a modernised monarchy able to carry out sweeping reform.

state-harmful.rationale: Cameralism exists to strengthen the state and its administration, and treats the state as the instrument of public happiness.

empower-police-military.rationale: Seckendorff and Justi made security and a strong army essential to the state's power, and Polizei was the era's main domestic administrative arm.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: A cameralist writer in Small's survey would tolerate regulated brothels for reasons of state while moral writers condemned them, so adherents split.

decide-locally.rationale: Cameralism arose to centralise and standardise administration in each territory under the prince's collegial bodies, against estates and local privileges.

rehabilitation.rationale: Cameralists favoured workhouses to make idlers productive and discussed penal reform, but also harsh policing; Justi-era writers differed on punishment.

traditional-family.rationale: Cameralist writers treated the household and marriage as the base of Oeconomie and promoted marriage and large families to raise population.

more-religion-public.rationale: Cameralists considered religion a state concern and ruler duty, but Justi and Jung-Stilling stressed toleration and keeping religion useful to civil welfare; adherents ranged from pietist to enlightened.

gradual-change.rationale: Cameralists were reforming officials who wanted sweeping administrative change by royal decree, yet also worked through existing institutions and warned against abrupt changes. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Cameralists wanted population growth and actively encouraged skilled immigration and settlement as a source of state wealth.

free-trade.rationale: Cameralism resembled mercantilism with import substitution and protection of domestic manufactures; Justi sought removal of some domestic bans but a favourable foreign balance.

open-borders.rationale: Cameralist states controlled movement and keeping subjects within the territory was part of population policy, even as they welcomed selected immigrants.

limit-growth.rationale: Increasing production, population and national wealth was the central aim of cameralism. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Cameralist training covered natural sciences, mining and husbandry, and officials expected improved technique and manufactures to increase wealth.

revolution-justified.rationale: Cameralism is the administrative doctrine of the absolute monarch and treats subjects' duty of obedience as basic; Justi sought reform from above.

experts-over-public.rationale: Cameralism trained a professional civil service in a science of administration to run the state, and distrusted individuals' capacity to know what serves the public welfare.

central-planning.rationale: Cameralists wanted comprehensive state management of production but within a private-and-crown economy of household production, not a planned economy in the modern sense; adherents split on reading.

socialized-markets.rationale: The question assumes worker or public ownership with markets; cameralists accepted markets under state direction but not worker ownership, so a mild disagree.

land-value-tax.rationale: Cameralist fiscal policy used crown domains, regalia and a range of taxes, and Justi wrote on balanced tax systems rather than a single tax on land.

basic-income.rationale: Cameralist welfare meant organised care for the poor tied to compulsory work in workhouses; unconditional payment contradicts their view that idlers be put to work.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Import substitution, protection of domestic manufactures and a favourable balance of trade were central cameralist instruments.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Cameralists had the prince establish manufactures, mines and trading companies, giving credit and privileges to strategic industries.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Cameralism aimed at accumulating money and wealth in the state; abolishing money would contradict its fiscal science (Kameral).

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Cameralists managed money, coinage and credit as state business, so leaving money to the market contradicts their approach.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Cameralist states supervised guilds that set prices and wages, but tripartite bargaining bodies as modern corporatism did not exist; adherents like Justi also wanted guild power reduced.

one-party-rule.rationale: No parties existed; cameralism assumed monarchical rule through a collegial bureaucracy, not a single ideological party, so mild disagreement.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a monarch who rules, and the statement now asks only about a ceremonial head of state, on which the sources cited here are silent.

reviewHistory.rationale: Cameralism is the science of managing the monarchical state, and Justi held a modernised monarchy was the only form able to carry through economic reform.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about a monarch who rules, and the statement now asks only about a ceremonial head of state, on which the sources cited here are silent.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

democracy-best.rationale: Cameralists favoured absolutist or paternalist monarchy for the welfare of subjects; Justi concluded monarchy was best for reform, though he opposed despotism.

direct-votes.rationale: Cameralism rests on administration by trained officials under the sovereign; popular votes on laws find no place.

workers-councils.rationale: Political power rested in the monarch and his colleges of officials; workers' councils are foreign to cameralism. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

right-to-secede.rationale: Cameralism built larger more efficient territorial states and Justi wanted bigger German states to rival France and England, so secession cuts against it.

natural-rulers.rationale: Cameralists assumed rule by the prince and his educated officials, and the gentry were to be educated in estate management; birth and training qualified rulers.

political-violence-never.rationale: Cameralist authors treated state force as legitimate for security and war while rejecting rebellion, so the statement's blanket form splits them.

war-builds-character.rationale: Cameralists valued military power as a function of the state's wealth, but Justi wrote against the European balance as a source of wars; character-building is not their argument.

separate-church-state.rationale: Cameralist national management included religion and morals, and the prince supervised the church, though Justi and Jung-Stilling favoured toleration of non-harmful faiths.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Cameralism rested on natural law and the sovereign's reason with Christian principles as a moral guide for Polizei, not on scriptural law as such; Seckendorff was more religious than Justi.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Courts, policing and defence were core sovereign functions in the cameralist state. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

military-superiority.rationale: Cameralists aimed to raise state revenue and power to rival other states in military strength.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Territorial states in the Empire were multi-ethnic dynastic states, and cameralists welcomed immigrants of any origin who added to the population.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Cameralism held that the interests of ruler and people align and that estates should be harmonised under the sovereign. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Cameralist society was ordered by estates with differentiated duties; the aim was general happiness and prosperity, not equality.

civilizational-union.rationale: Cameralists worked within separate German territorial states and did not propose unions by civilization; Justi wanted larger states, but within the Empire.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Cameralists held that individuals cannot be trusted and that officials guide subjects toward the common good, though Justi saw ruler and subjects' happiness as linked.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Cameralist and Pietist texts stress duties of subjects and rulers, though Jung-Stilling speaks of 'rights of humanity' that the state protects as well.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Cameralists treated nature as a resource for state revenue, forestry and farming; intrinsic value is a modern idea.

limit-population.rationale: Population increase was a central cameralist goal, as the source of labour, soldiers and tax revenue.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Cameralists sought to spread manufactures and raise output, regarding them as sources of national wealth.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Cameralists promoted manufactures and applied science but within an ordered administrative framework, so an agree without 'disrupting institutions' emphasis.

restore-past-order.rationale: Cameralists were reformers building a more efficient modern state against the older estate-based order; they wanted progress in administration and prosperity.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Cameralism was a practical administrative science judged by revenue, population and welfare outcomes rather than by doctrine.

direct-action.rationale: Change was to come from the sovereign and his officials; subjects acting on their own was disorder. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Cameralism was about raising productivity through agriculture, mining, and manufactures. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Cameralists encouraged manufactures, trades and specialised industries as means to wealth.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Cameralists wanted help for the needy but set work as a duty ('he who does not work is not worthy to eat'), with property distributed through existing orders.

production-for-use.rationale: Cameralists sought production for state and subject welfare yet relied on markets, money and profit by artisans and merchants; split.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The exploitation theory is a later socialist doctrine; cameralists saw trade and manufacture profits as sources of national wealth.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Foreign to a doctrine of monarchical administration with estates under the prince. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

collective-farming.rationale: Cameralists wanted to improve private peasant and domain agriculture through state encouragement, not collectivise it.

taxation-theft.rationale: Revenue extraction was the core of Kameral science, and Justi wrote guidelines for taxation to strengthen the state.

harm-principle.rationale: Cameralist Polizei regulated morals and conduct for the subjects' happiness; Jung-Stilling allows liberty only so far as it harms no one but also expects the state to promote perfection.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Jung-Stilling speaks of rights of humanity (person, property, honour, liberty) for individuals while cameralists emphasised duties and estates; unresolved.

conscription.rationale: Seckendorff-era writers argued for universal military duty, as shown in Small's survey, and cameralist states drew soldiers from the population.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Cameralists sought to retain and enlarge the population and regarded emigration as a loss. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Cameralists considered administrative science to be rational and teachable knowledge to improve the state; the postmodern claim is foreign.

universal-morality.rationale: Justi tied cameralism to natural law, and Jung-Stilling derives the state's purpose from natural rights knowable to reason and Christian morals.

single-common-good.rationale: Cameralism assumes a single common welfare and happiness that the ruler and educated officials determine, not a balancing of interests.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Administration was hierarchical in the cameralist state; workers' or public votes in running enterprises are foreign to it.

economic-freedom.rationale: Cameralists did not make political liberty depend on economic liberty; their model joined state direction of the economy with an obedient monarchy.

rule-by-example.rationale: Seckendorff's Christian princely mirror stressed the ruler's own virtue but Polizei and law were the main means, so the answer is split.

national-self-determination.rationale: Cameralist loyalty was to the dynastic territorial state; self-determination of nations is a later idea.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Justi's cameralism followed natural law and Enlightenment rationalism, while Seckendorff and Jung-Stilling gave Christian faith a central role; adherents are split.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Cameralists made vagrants and idlers work and held that those who do not work should not eat; workhouses were typical.

class-collaboration.rationale: Cameralists held ruler, estates and subjects to share an interest in general happiness and wanted guild and trade groups subordinated to common welfare.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Cameralists founded libraries, universities and academies to train officials and for national management; destroying heritage was no goal.

ban-interest.rationale: Cameralists ran credit institutions such as banks and montes pietatis and treated money circulation as a state interest, not interest bans.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Cameralists valued population growth and welcomed settlers and no cameralist source classifies subjects by race.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Cameralism presents the state as serving the common happiness of all subjects, not any one class.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy theory with no place in cameralist sources, which welcomed population growth by immigration. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

proportional-representation.rationale: Cameralism assumed no elected legislature at all; the principle of proportional party representation is foreign, so a mild disagree.

national-mission.rationale: Cameralist aims were internal prosperity and territorial strength, not spreading a form of government abroad.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Cameralists staked their programme on the competence and honesty of trained officials, and Justi proposed colleges to keep the ruler virtuous.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: No cameralist source supports it; their population policy was pro-natalist, although regulation of marriage was normal.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Cameralists made the state manage the economy, morals, education and welfare, far beyond defence and justice.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: No cameralist source supports it and population growth was prized.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Jung-Stilling affirms natural rights for all and Seckendorff said salvation is equal for peasant and king, while civil status stayed unequal by estate. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Jung-Stilling allows religious parties to continue as long as they cause no harm, while others of the period restricted sects; split.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Cameralists encouraged livestock husbandry and meat and hide production as agricultural wealth; the idea of a ban is foreign.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Christian education of subjects was a Polizei duty in the cameralist state.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A socialist state is outside this ideology, but the state's strength against rivals is a general cameralist premise; no direct view.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Justi's idea was that people entrusted collective pursuit of happiness to one ruler, a contract-like origin; legitimacy rests on serving welfare rather than present consent.

trade-surplus.rationale: A favourable balance of foreign trade was one of Justi's three sources of national wealth and cameralism is mercantilist in this.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Cameralism emphasised administrative order and cooperation under the ruler, though states competed for power.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Cameralism accepted the monarch's discretionary power, restrained by moral virtue and administrative colleges rather than law-based non-domination.

separated-powers.rationale: Justi was influenced by Montesquieu and proposed colleges, but cameralists kept the prince as sole source of power; split.

vanguard-party.rationale: Foreign to cameralism, which relies on the prince's bureaucracy. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Care for the poor was a state task, but the aim was common happiness and productive employment, not priority to any group.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Cameralists held that a larger population is the source of wealth and power, not of poverty.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Cameralists welcomed settlers and skilled immigrants of various religions and origins, so diversity was not seen as a threat.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Cameralist offices were filled by educated officials appointed by the ruler, trained by cameralist courses.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The sovereign had full discretion in states of necessity in the absolutist state, though Jung-Stilling stresses rights, so a modest agree.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Polizei regulated grain, bread and meat prices and provisioning, and magazines against scarcity were standard cameralist practice, though Justi favoured freer grain export in good times.

party-controls-media.rationale: No party existed, but cameralists backed book censorship and state control of printing; Jung-Stilling wanted police limits on harmful publications.

party-commands-army.rationale: No parties; the prince commanded the army through his officials.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Cameralist states sought to attract settlers and speedy subject status to raise population.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: No legislature of elected representatives exists in the model; officials were salaried by rank.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Parties are outside cameralism, and nothing supports a side.

head-commands-forces.rationale: In the cameralist monarchy the sovereign commanded the army and chose his ministers and college officials.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Cameralists across Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic territories differed, and Justi converted to Catholicism; no common position.

clerical-rule.rationale: The prince and his civil administration ruled, with religion supervised as one branch of Polizei; clerics had no highest authority.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Subjects owe obedience to the sovereign, who directs the war effort. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Cameralist Polizei supervised book censorship and public morals, and Jung-Stilling wants police to prevent harmful publications and theatre.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Presidents do not exist in the cameralist model; the monarch ruled for life, so the question does not separate adherents.

recall-officials.rationale: Officials answered to the sovereign and his colleges, not to voters, so recall by voters is foreign.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Cameralist states sought military strength and Justi criticised a balance-of-power doctrine, but alliances were normal tools of princely policy.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: The state ordering of towns, markets and property did not abolish tenancies; cameralist urban policy supervised rents and lodging.

people-in-arms.rationale: Cameralist writers proposed universal duty for military service but organised armies under state discipline, so a citizens' militia replacing the army is a mild disagree.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Agriculture was the base of state wealth for the cameralists, who valued peasants, but they also promoted towns and manufactures.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Cameralism put university-trained officials at the heart of government and founded professorships to train them. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

death-penalty.rationale: Cameralist-era writers differed on executions; Jung-Stilling treats it as an open question, and Sonnenfels argued against it as against the aims of the state. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Polizei suppressed indecent publications and prostitution outside regulation as part of state control of morals.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Jung-Stilling tolerates harmless sects but limits any teaching or practice that damages civil society, and the state sets common law.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Cameralist Polizei sought to shape subjects' morals and habits and assumed that people could not be trusted to rule themselves.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Constitutions were not drafted by assemblies; the monarch and his administration fixed the order. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Cameralism assumes that the sovereign may direct subjects and curb liberties to build the state's wealth and strength.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: The head of state was a hereditary monarch in the cameralist state. No cited source addresses this statement directly.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Currency and finance were state business of the ruler's treasury (Kameral), not placed in an independent body.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Cameralist doctrine subordinated individual economic action to common welfare, even as Justi respected private property.

collective-defense.rationale: Alliances were tools of princely policy and Justi doubted the European balance; no clear position.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Dynastic states acquired territory by conquest and treaty, without any test of consent of the people.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Cameralist national management included religion, and the prince supervised church affairs; Justi clashed with ecclesiastical authorities.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The monarch ruled actively in cameralism rather than standing above politics as a symbol, but he did stand above parties, so no clear answer.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Cameralists built and consolidated strong territorial states, and the prince would defend its integrity by force.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Cameralism aimed at standardising law and the economy in a state, so a region keeping a separate system runs against it.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Seckendorff's ruler is an office holder with duties before God, and Justi's ruler serves subjects' welfare, neither sacred nor divine in descent.

character-from-environment.rationale: Cameralists believed education, Polizei and good management could shape subjects' industry and morals.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Absolute rule was assumed, but Seckendorff and Justi demanded rulers' duties and Justi's colleges checked the ruler's virtue; adherents are split.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Justi weighed constitutions after Montesquieu but concluded modern monarchy was best for reform, not a balance of few and many.

leader-cult.rationale: Cameralists valued the ruler's moral example and duty but not mass praise; the question is a modern one.

organic-representation.rationale: Cameralism had no representation by parties; the prince's colleges administered, and it sought to reduce guild and estate privilege (Justi), so corporate representation is not a feature.

total-state.rationale: Cameralist national management covered morals, education, religion and the economy more directly than later economic liberalism, though it was not a modern totalitarian claim.

national-rebirth.rationale: Cameralists were administrative reformers rather than regeneration movements; the rhetoric of decadence and rebirth is not found in the sources.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Justi aimed for German states to rival England and France in power, but cameralism chiefly stressed internal development; split.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Cameralism replaced feudal personal ties with a salaried bureaucracy of trained officials.

bound-labor.rationale: Cameralist writers sought productive peasants and agrarian improvement, and Justi attacked guild and feudal hindrances, though serfdom still existed in their states.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The cameralist state relies on compulsion in taxes, Polizei, conscription and workhouses for common welfare.

ban-cartels.rationale: Cameralists curbed some guild privileges yet granted state monopolies and manufactories; adherents were split, so neutral.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Import substitution and a favourable trade balance are described as core cameralist economic policy, supporting a self-sufficient bloc.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: A strong hereditary monarch and a ranked society are the premise of the cameralist state, so abolishing hereditary privilege contradicts its core.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Cameralist texts concern administration and finance; they did not teach a civilization-centred history, so this is neutral.

elective-rulers.rationale: Cameralism sets trained officials under a strong hereditary monarch whose duty is subjects' welfare; election of rulers is not part of it.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Cameralism is a science of ruling for the monarch through his officials; a supreme parliament is the opposite of its design.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist trade-balance thinking sees trade as moving wealth between states, but cameralists blamed poor policy, not a world structure; adherents give no clear answer.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Cameralism served an absolute monarch and entrusted rule to trained officials, with no place for mandated or recallable representatives.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Cameralism served the prince's finances under absolutism; the ruler and his officials, not an assembly, controlled revenue and spending.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Cameralists favoured luxury production for trade balance, though sumptuary regulation was also part of Polizei; split.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Raising population was a central cameralist goal because people produced revenue and output for the state.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: It places a strong monarch and trained officials over subjects, who owe obedience.

local-production.rationale: It favoured national self-sufficiency and import substitution, which is not the same as local production.

informal-organisation.rationale: It rests on a bureaucracy and the monarch's state, not informal groups.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Cameralists defended subjects' private property while the prince's domains and monopolies were state-run; the common-ownership half of the claim is not cameralist, so this is split.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Cameralist writers mostly wrote in German or Latin and some, like Justi, defended clear German prose, but no purge policy is documented, so this is neutral.

treaties-binding.rationale: Cameralism concerned absolutist territorial states with no doctrine on treaties with internal nations; its priority on the prince's authority and the state's interest points both ways.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Cameralist absolutism put order under the ruler and the police, and the textbooks set limits on press and associations.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The Polizei state supervised religion and allowed only limited toleration of religious parties.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Cameralism put government in the hands of trained officials under a strong monarch, not in direct popular decision-making.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Cameralists backed standing armies and conscription as tools of state power and revenue.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Cameralism served hereditary territorial monarchs and took dynastic rule for granted as the frame for the trained bureaucracy.

property-franchise.rationale: Cameralists did not discuss voting; subjects were ruled by officials under a monarch, and property was respected but not tied to a franchise.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Cameralists valued orderly administration and codified Polizei ordinances, but upheld the ruler's discretionary decree power under absolutism.

racial-franchise.rationale: Cameralism had no racial franchise doctrine; its concern was population and subjects' welfare, and it did not set racial limits on office.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Cameralist writers allowed limited toleration of religious parties while states of the era often restricted mixed marriage; the tradition did not settle the matter.

rent-control.rationale: Cameralist Polizei regulated prices and economic life in the interest of welfare; rent caps are an inference from that tradition.

independent-unions.rationale: Unions did not exist, but cameralists put guilds and trades under state regulation and Justi reduced guild power, so autonomous bodies were not favoured.

family-wage.rationale: Cameralists regulated wages and prices and cared for the population, but a family wage was never put forward as a principle.

person-over-state.rationale: Justi and Jung-Stilling held that the state's purpose is subjects' welfare and spoke of rights of humanity, yet the ruler's wealth and power remained the aim; adherents were split.

dense-cities.rationale: Cameralists promoted manufacture and population but gave no environmental view of cities, so this is neutral.

racial-pride.rationale: The concept of racial pride does not appear in cameralist writing, which attached loyalty to the prince and state.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Mercantilist rivalry between states was assumed, but the sources describe no partition-plot theme.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Cameralism is the science of building and running the bureaucratic state under a strong monarch, so destroying that machinery is the opposite of its aims.

sacred-nation.rationale: Cameralism was loyal to the prince and territorial state, not to a sacred nation, which is a later notion.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Student loans did not exist, and cameralists favoured training officials at state expense but never discussed debt relief.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Cameralists regulated property and inheritance under Polizei and civil law, but the sources do not give a position on equal inheritance for women; adherents split.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Cameralist Polizei limited the press and policed public order as a state duty; extending this to modern communications is an inference.

race-social-construct.rationale: Race as a concept is not treated in the cameralist sources; neither answer can be derived from its principles.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Cameralists were Lutheran or Catholic officials, but their science of administration took no position on scriptural literalism.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Cameralists made care for the poor and the productive employment of subjects a state duty, though with work compulsion for idlers; cutting welfare for dependency reasons is not their line. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: The state should actively promote population growth as a source of national strength and wealth.
missingStatements.rationale: Population increase as the basis of labour, soldiers and revenue runs through the cameralist writers surveyed by Small and is one of Justi's three sources of wealth.

missingStatements.text: The ruler's chief duty is to promote the happiness and welfare of his subjects.
missingStatements.rationale: Justi wrote that no one can rule free and reasonable beings except to promote their welfare, and cameralism was the economics of public happiness.
missingStatements.declined: Near-universal claim that most governments would accept, so it would not separate ideologies.

missingStatements.text: Government should raise revenue chiefly from state-owned land, mines and enterprises rather than from taxes on subjects.
missingStatements.rationale: Cameralist public finance (Kameral) rested on crown domains, regalia and state enterprises, with taxes secondary.
missingStatements.declined: Specific to early-modern public finance; public-ownership covers state enterprise loosely.

missingStatements.text: Government should require idle and vagrant people to work.
missingStatements.rationale: Cameralists supported workhouses and compulsory labour for idlers and held that who does not work should not eat.
missingStatements.declined: Covered loosely by work-for-welfare; narrow to early-modern poor-law practice.

notes: Cameralists differed over time: Seckendorff was a Christian princely moralist, Justi an Enlightened natural-law reformer who curbed guilds, and Jung-Stilling a late Pietist writing about rights and toleration. Seckendorff and Sonnenfels have no sources opened beyond Small's survey.
